risks: With only 2 seeds, per-class accuracy differences may fall within random seed noise and be unreproducible with additional seeds.
Conclusions must be framed as exploratory because permutation inference is not valid with only 2 seeds, limiting publishability.
Fashion-MNIST's 1,000-image per class test set means per-class accuracy estimates have standard errors of approximately 0.6–0.9 percentage points.
title: Per-class accuracy impact of augmentation on Fashion-MNIST garments

impact.why: Explains the mechanism behind aggregate accuracy changes and provides actionable guidance about which garment classes benefit from each augmentation type.

novelty.why: None of the prior works examine per-class accuracy deltas from basic image augmentation specifically on Fashion-MNIST, nor do they analyze how horizontal-flip augmentation differentially affects morphologically similar or asymmetric garment classes (e.g., shirt vs. T-shirt/top). The closest works address class-wise augmentation effects in other domains (batik motifs, liver lesions) but not this specific dataset or hypothesis about flip-induced label ambiguity.

feasibility.why: Analysis is derived entirely from models already trained in the core experiment, requiring only CPU-based inference and plotting with no additional GPU runs.

testability.why: Per-class accuracy delta is directly measurable from stored predictions, though with 2 seeds significance assessment is limited to exploratory framing.

approach: Extract per-class precision, recall, F1, and full confusion matrices from augmented and non-augmented trained models across seeds 42 and 123 (four models total). Compute Δaccuracy and Δconfusion-cell for each of the 10 classes and each of the 100 class pairs, then visualize as a per-class accuracy delta bar chart and annotated delta confusion matrix; all analysis runs on CPU using stored model predictions from the core experiment's GPU runs.
question: Does basic image augmentation disproportionately improve or reduce accuracy on specific Fashion-MNIST garment classes, particularly for morphologically similar or asymmetric classes?
why_open: (Yee 2026) notes that morphologically distinctive categories such as trousers, bags, and footwear show high discriminative performance but does not study how augmentation changes per-class accuracy. All papers reporting augmentation effects on Fashion-MNIST (Greeshma et al. 2019; Mukhamediev 2024; Hassan et al. 2025; Kayed et al. 2020) aggregate accuracy into a single number, obscuring which garment classes drive gains or losses. (Agarwal et al. 2025) found that augmentation did not consistently improve accuracy for the best-performing model on CIFAR-10, suggesting class-level heterogeneity, but no analogous per-class study exists for Fashion-MNIST. Fashion-MNIST has known confusable class pairs such as T-shirt versus shirt versus pullover where flip-induced distortions might introduce label-ambiguous training examples and hurt recognition.
hypothesis: Augmentation will disproportionately help symmetric garment classes (trousers, pullovers, coats) for which horizontal flips are valid invariances, while potentially reducing accuracy for fine-grained confusable classes such as shirt versus T-shirt/top where flipped images introduce label ambiguity.
data_needed: Fashion-MNIST test set (10,000 images, 10 balanced classes); predictions from the four trained models produced in the core experiment.
